title: Arrays, objects, immutability
blurb: Copying, mutation, array methods, Map and Set. The material behind every 'why did unrelated state change?' bug.

questions.why: Spread is a shallow copy: `b.user` and `a.user` are the same object, so the write shows through `a`. 'Ada' is the answer people expect when they think spread copies every level; for that use `structuredClone(a)`, or copy each level you intend to change.
questions.asked: This is the React state bug in its purest form, and the follow-up is always 'so how do you update a nested field correctly?'.

questions.q: Which produces a new array with the item at index 2 replaced, leaving `items` untouched?
choices: `items.splice(2, 1, next)` and use its return value
questions.why: map always returns a new array. `copy = items` copies the reference, not the array; splice mutates and returns the *removed* elements; fill mutates and returns the same array. ES2023 also gives `items.with(2, next)` for exactly this.
questions.asked: Replacing one row in a list held as state is daily React work; interviewers want the non-mutating version without a pause.

choices: Removes the elements that fail a predicate
Shortens the array in place to a given length
Merges adjacent duplicates into single items
Folds the array into one accumulated value
questions.why: `reduce((acc, item) => next, initial)` threads an accumulator through every element and returns the final value. Removing elements that fail a test is `filter`. reduce can express map and filter, but use those when they say it more clearly.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually 'implement groupBy with reduce', which shows whether you can actually drive the accumulator.

questions.code:
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
const doubled = nums.map((n) => { n * 2; });
choices: An empty array, since nothing is returned
questions.why: Braces make the arrow a block body, and a block body with no `return` returns undefined, so map collects three undefineds. map still produces one slot per element, which is why it is not empty. Drop the braces or add `return`.
questions.asked: A two-second bug in code review that still costs people ten minutes in the debugger; it checks you read arrow syntax precisely.

questions.q: Which expression removes duplicate numbers from an array?
questions.why: A Set keeps one of each value (SameValueZero equality) in insertion order, and spreading it back gives an array. `filter(Boolean)` only drops falsy values, `Object.keys` returns the index strings, and `new Map(items)` throws because numbers are not [key, value] entries.
questions.asked: The warm-up before the harder follow-up: deduplicating objects, where a Set no longer works.

questions.code:
const set = new Set([{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]);
console.log(set.size);
questions.why: Set compares objects by reference, and two object literals are two different objects even with identical contents. To deduplicate records, key them: `new Map(items.map((i) => [i.id, i]))`.
questions.asked: The natural follow-up to the dedupe question, and it catches a lot of people.

questions.q: What is the difference between `find` and `filter`?
choices: find returns the index of the first match; filter returns the matches
find throws when nothing matches; filter returns an empty array
find returns the first match; filter returns an array of all matches
find returns every match as an iterator; filter returns an array
questions.why: find short-circuits and returns the element itself, or undefined when nothing matches; returning the index is `findIndex`. Using `filter(...)[0]` works but scans the whole array and allocates one you throw away.
questions.asked: Checks you pick the method that says what you mean, and that you know find returns undefined rather than throwing.

questions.code: console.log(Object.keys({ 2: 'b', 1: 'a', x: 'c' }));
questions.why: Integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order. So insertion order is not preserved for id-like keys; use a Map or an array when order matters.
questions.asked: It comes up when someone stores an ordered list in an object keyed by id and the order changes.

questions.q: How do you reliably check whether an object has its own property `key`?
questions.why: `in` also finds inherited keys, and the undefined check cannot tell a missing key from one set to undefined. `obj.hasOwnProperty` is the tempting one: it throws on `Object.create(null)` objects and can be shadowed by an own `hasOwnProperty` key from parsed input. `Object.hasOwn` (ES2022) has neither problem.
questions.asked: It separates people who have been bitten by untrusted keys from people who learned the old idiom and stopped there.

choices: 1, because `__proto__` is an ordinary own key
Object.prototype, because the write is ignored
NaN, because an object plus 1 is not a number
undefined, because the setter deletes the key
questions.why: __proto__ is an accessor on Object.prototype. The read returns Object.prototype (truthy, so || 0 never fires), the sum is the string '[object Object]1', and the setter ignores any non-object value, so the key is never written. Node prints that value as [Object: null prototype] {}. A word counter over user input silently breaks on this word; use a Map or Object.create(null).
questions.asked: It is the concrete reason 'use a Map for a lookup keyed by user input' is real advice, not style.

choices: Maps each element, then flattens the result by one level
Flattens nested arrays fully, then maps each element
Maps each element and drops any that return null
Maps each element into a Map keyed by the result
questions.why: flatMap is `map` followed by `flat(1)`. Returning `[]` from the callback drops an element and returning `[value]` keeps it, so it expresses 'map some, skip others' in one pass. It does not drop null by itself; you return `[]` for that.
questions.asked: A signal of fluency with the array API; the strong answer mentions the map-and-filter-in-one-pass use.

questions.why: `length` is writable, and shrinking it deletes the elements past the new length in place. Holes appear only when you grow `length`, which is where the empty-items output comes from.
questions.asked: An old way to clear an array that still shows up in legacy code; knowing it mutates in place matters when that array is shared.

questions.q: Which adds `newItem` to the front of `items` without mutating it?
questions.why: Spread with the new item first builds a fresh array in the right order. `concat` appends to the end, splice mutates, and `[...items].unshift(newItem)` copies correctly but returns the new *length*, not the array.
questions.asked: Prepending to a list in React state is common, and the unshift-returns-a-number trap catches people who half know the answer.

questions.q: What is wrong with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` as a deep clone?
choices: It copies only the top level, so nested objects stay shared
It keeps Dates and Maps but drops every function and symbol
Dates become strings, Maps and undefined vanish, cycles throw
It works on anything but is too slow for objects over 1 MB
questions.why: The round trip only survives what JSON can express: Dates become ISO strings, Map and Set become `{}`, undefined-valued keys disappear and a cycle throws. It is deep, which is why people trust it. `structuredClone` handles Dates, Maps, Sets and cycles (not functions).
questions.asked: Everyone has used this trick; the question is whether you know its limits.

questions.code: console.log([1, 2, 3].includes(NaN), [NaN].includes(NaN), [NaN].indexOf(NaN));
questions.why: includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to itself. indexOf uses strict equality, and NaN !== NaN, so it can never find one.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know the array methods do not all share one equality rule.

questions.q: Which groups `items` into lists keyed by `type`?
questions.why: `Object.groupBy` (ES2024, Node 21+) returns `{ [type]: item[] }`. The fromEntries and Map versions build a key per type but keep only the *last* item for each. The array method was proposed and renamed to a static for web compatibility, so `items.groupBy` does not exist.
questions.asked: A very common live-coding warm-up; the follow-up is to write it with reduce and `acc[key] ??= []`.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Object.entries` and `Object.getOwnPropertyNames`?
choices: entries includes inherited keys; getOwnPropertyNames only own ones
entries skips non-enumerable keys; getOwnPropertyNames includes them
entries includes symbol keys; getOwnPropertyNames only string ones
entries returns only values; getOwnPropertyNames returns key names
questions.why: Both look only at own string keys. entries skips non-enumerable ones and returns [key, value] pairs; getOwnPropertyNames returns names including non-enumerable ones (such as an array's `length`). Neither sees symbol keys, and `Object.values` is the values-only one.
questions.asked: Enumerability explains why some properties vanish from spreads, logs and JSON; this is the entry point to that conversation.

questions.why: sort mutates and returns the same array reference. So `const sorted = state.sort()` mutates your state and hands the same object back, which React then treats as unchanged. `toSorted()` (ES2023) returns a copy.
questions.asked: A great one-liner for testing whether someone understands referential equality.

questions.q: When would you use a `WeakMap` over a `Map`?
choices: To attach data to objects without keeping them from being collected
To look up string keys faster than a Map once the table grows large
To store entries that you need to iterate later in insertion order
To hold keys by value, so that mutating a key object cannot affect it
questions.why: A WeakMap holds its keys weakly: an entry disappears once nothing else references the key object. That is also why it only accepts objects as keys and cannot be iterated or sized, which rules out the string-key and iteration uses.
questions.asked: A memory-leak question in disguise: per-object caches in a plain Map keep every object alive.

questions.why: map creates a new array but copies the same references into it. To copy each row too: `rows.map((row) => ({ ...row }))`.
questions.asked: The 'I did copy it' bug: the array is new, the contents are not.

questions.q: The first line logs 6. What does the second line do?
questions.code:
console.log([1, 2, 3].reduce((a, b) => a + b));
console.log([].reduce((a, b) => a + b));
questions.why: Without an initial value, reduce uses the first element as the accumulator, and an empty array has none, so it throws 'Reduce of empty array with no initial value'. It cannot know 0 is the identity for your callback. Always pass the initial value; it also fixes the accumulator's type.
questions.asked: A total over a filtered list that happens to be empty is a classic production crash.

questions.q: Each item's `date` is a `Date`. Which returns the items newest first without mutating `items`?
questions.why: A comparator must return a number; Dates subtract cleanly to milliseconds. A boolean coerces to 0 or 1 and never says 'a before b', so the order is wrong. `sort` mutates `items`, and Dates have no `localeCompare` (that works on ISO strings). `toSorted` is ES2023.
questions.asked: Returning a boolean from a comparator is a surprisingly common bug that mostly works on small arrays.

questions.code: const { id, ...rest } = { id: 1, a: 2, b: 3 };
choices: An array of the remaining values, `[2, 3]`
A copy of everything, `{ id: 1, a: 2, b: 3 }`
questions.why: Object rest collects the remaining own enumerable properties into a new object, a shallow copy without `id`; the source is not modified. Array rest is what gives an array. It is the idiomatic 'omit a key', and how components forward props: `const { className, ...rest } = props`.
questions.asked: Everyday syntax in React code; the interviewer wants 'new object, source untouched'.

questions.q: Why does `{ a: 1 } === { a: 1 }` evaluate to false?
choices: `===` only compares contents for frozen objects
The literals get different hidden prototypes
Number values inside objects are compared as strings
questions.why: Every object literal creates a new object, and `===` (and `==`) compare objects by identity. Comparing contents means a deep-equal or a canonical key. It is also why an inline object in a React dependency array re-runs the effect every render.
questions.asked: It links directly to the React useEffect dependency question.

questions.why: `toSorted` and `with` (ES2023) are the copying versions of `sort` and index assignment: each returns a new array and leaves `a` alone. `with(0, 9)` replaces index 0; it does not insert. `toReversed` and `toSpliced` complete the set.
questions.asked: These methods exist precisely for immutable state updates; knowing them signals current JavaScript, not 2015 JavaScript.

questions.why: `[1, , 3]` has a hole at index 1: the length is 3 but there is no element there. forEach, map, filter and reduce skip holes, while `for...of` and `Array.from` visit them as undefined. Holes also come from `new Array(n)` and from growing `length`.
questions.asked: It explains the classic `new Array(5).map(...)` does-nothing bug, which is the practical version of this question.

questions.q: Which returns a new object with every value of `prices` doubled?
questions.why: entries turns the object into [key, value] pairs, map transforms them, and fromEntries (ES2019) builds a new object. The forEach version passes undefined to fromEntries and throws; the other two return arrays of one-key objects, and `{ k: ... }` uses the literal key 'k'.
questions.asked: Transforming a keyed object is a constant chore with API payloads; this idiom is the one reviewers expect.

questions.why: `Array.from` accepts any array-like, and `{ length: 5 }` is one, so the map function runs for each index. `new Array(5)` is five holes, which `map` skips; `Array.of(5)` is `[5]`; and a number is not array-like, so `Array.from(5)` is `[]`.
questions.asked: Building a range for pagination buttons or test fixtures comes up constantly, and the `new Array(n).map` trap is common.

questions.q: An order has no items yet. What does this log?
questions.code:
const items = [];
console.log(items.every((i) => i.shipped), items.some((i) => i.shipped));
questions.why: `every` on an empty array is true (no element fails) and `some` is false (no element passes). So an 'all items shipped' badge lights up on an empty order unless you also check `items.length > 0`.
questions.asked: Empty-collection edge cases are where validation and status logic go wrong; interviewers use this to see if you think about them.

questions.q: What happens when a `forEach` callback runs `return` on the first invalid row?
choices: It stops the loop, like `break` in a for loop
It skips that row and moves on to the next one
It stops the loop and forEach returns that row
It throws, because forEach callbacks cannot return
questions.why: `return` only ends that one call of the callback; forEach keeps calling it for every element and always returns undefined. To stop early use `for...of` with `break`, or `some`/`find`, which stop at the first truthy result.
questions.asked: It checks that you understand forEach is a function call per element, not loop syntax.

questions.code:
const cache = { users: new Map([['u1', 'Ada']]) };
console.log(JSON.stringify(cache));
questions.why: JSON.stringify only serialises own enumerable properties, and a Map keeps its entries internally, so it becomes `{}` silently. Convert first: `Object.fromEntries(map)` for an object or `[...map]` for pairs.
questions.asked: Caching or sending a Map over the wire and getting `{}` back is a real bug; this checks you would know why.

questions.why: Spread copies every own enumerable property, including ones whose value is undefined, so the later `size: undefined` overwrites the default. Destructuring defaults skip undefined; spread does not. Strip undefined keys first or merge with `??`.
questions.asked: Merging defaults with parsed query options is everywhere, and this is how a page size silently becomes undefined.

questions.q: A user lookup finds nothing. What does this log?
questions.code:
const users = [{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }];
console.log(users.find((u) => u.id === 3), users.findIndex((u) => u.id === 3));
questions.why: `find` returns `undefined` when nothing matches (never `null` or an empty array), and `findIndex` returns -1. Check for `undefined` before using the result, or the next line throws.
questions.asked: It checks you know the "not found" value of each method, which decides how you guard the result.

questions.q: A tag list from a form contains blanks. What does this log?
questions.code:
const tags = ['sale', '', null, 'new', 0, 'eco'];
console.log(tags.filter(Boolean));
questions.why: `Boolean` is used as the predicate, so every falsy value (empty string, `null`, `0`, `NaN`, `undefined`, `false`) is removed. Watch out when 0 is a legitimate value, such as a quantity, because it is dropped too.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions the 0 trap, which turns a neat idiom into a data-loss bug.

choices: It logs undefined, the last return value
It throws a TypeError on the second item
questions.why: A block-bodied arrow needs an explicit `return`; without it the callback returns `undefined`, which becomes `acc` for the next item, and `undefined['u2'] = ...` throws. Add `return acc;` (or use `Object.fromEntries(users.map(...))`).
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see if you can spot the missing accumulator return, the most common `reduce` bug.

questions.code:
const lines = [{ qty: 2 }, { qty: 3 }];
console.log(lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.qty));
questions.why: With no initial value, `reduce` uses the first element (an object) as the accumulator and starts at the second, so `{ qty: 2 } + 3` becomes string concatenation. Always pass an initial value, here `0`, when the result type differs from the element type.
questions.asked: It checks you know why the initial value matters beyond the empty-array TypeError.

questions.code:
const nested = [1, [2, [3, [4]]]];
console.log(nested.flat(), nested.flat(Infinity));
questions.why: `flat()` flattens one level by default; pass a depth, or `Infinity` to flatten completely. It never mutates the original array.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know the default depth is 1, a frequent source of half-flattened data.

questions.q: Ids from a CSV are parsed, skipping bad values. What does this log?
questions.code:
const ids = ['1', 'x', '3'];
console.log(ids.flatMap((s) => (Number.isNaN(Number(s)) ? [] : [Number(s)])));
questions.why: `flatMap` flattens each returned array by one level, so returning `[]` drops an item and `[value]` keeps a transformed one. That filters and maps in a single pass.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it as a neat alternative to `filter` followed by `map` when the check and transform share work.

questions.q: A seating grid is initialised with `fill`. What does this log?
questions.why: `fill` puts the same value in every slot, and an array is a reference, so all three slots point at one array. Use `Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => [])` to create a new array per slot.
questions.asked: A strong answer names the fix with `Array.from` and the mapper function.

questions.why: `splice(start, deleteCount)` removes elements in place and returns the removed ones. Its second argument is a count, not an end index, which is where it differs from `slice`.
questions.asked: It checks you know `splice` mutates and what it returns, a common source of state bugs.

questions.code:
const items = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
console.log(items.slice(1), items.slice(-2, -1), items);
questions.why: `slice(start, end)` copies from `start` up to but not including `end`, and negative indexes count from the end. It never changes the original array.
questions.asked: A quick check of index arithmetic that paging and "show the last N" features rely on.

questions.code: console.log([1].concat(2, [3], [[4]]));
questions.why: `concat` spreads array arguments by exactly one level and appends other values as they are. So `[3]` contributes 3 but `[[4]]` contributes the inner array `[4]`.
questions.asked: It separates people who know `concat`'s one-level spreading from those who assume it flattens.

questions.code:
const slots = new Array(3);
console.log(slots.map(() => 'free'), Array.from(slots, () => 'free'));
questions.why: `new Array(3)` creates holes, not `undefined` values; `map` skips holes and keeps them in the output. `Array.from` iterates by index, reading holes as `undefined`, so its mapper runs three times.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see whether you know why `new Array(n).map(...)` "does nothing".

questions.why: `delete` removes the property but does not shift elements or change `length`, leaving a hole. Use `splice`, `filter` or `toSpliced` to actually remove an item.
questions.asked: It checks you would not use `delete` to remove array items, a classic junior mistake.

questions.q: A comparator returns a boolean. What does this log in Node 24?
questions.code:
const prices = [30, 5, 20, 10];
console.log(prices.toSorted((a, b) => a > b));
questions.why: A comparator must return a negative, zero or positive number. `a > b` gives `true`/`false`, which coerce to 1 and 0 and never say "a comes first", so V8 leaves this input unsorted. Use `a - b`.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains the three-way comparator contract instead of just saying "use a - b".

questions.why: Since ES2019, `Array.prototype.sort` is required to be stable: items that compare equal keep their original relative order. Cy came before Bo, so the two users stay in that order after the admin.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you know you can sort by a secondary key first and rely on stability.

questions.q: Which comparator sorts orders by `status` alphabetically, then by `total` highest first?
questions.why: `||` falls through to the second comparison only when the first returns 0 (equal status). `&&` does the opposite, the boolean version breaks the comparator contract, and swapping the order makes total the primary key.
questions.asked: Multi-key sorting is a standard take-home requirement for sortable tables.

questions.q: A React component calls `items.sort(byName)` on an array it received as a prop, during render. What is the problem?
choices: `sort` returns a new array, so the sorted result is thrown away
`sort` is asynchronous and finishes after the render completes
Arrays passed as props are frozen, so `sort` throws a TypeError
It sorts the parent's array in place, mutating state it does not own
questions.why: `sort` mutates in place and returns the same array, so the parent's state changes behind React's back and memoised children may not update. Use `items.toSorted(byName)` or `[...items].sort(byName)`.
questions.asked: A strong answer names `toSorted` and explains why reference equality makes in-place changes invisible.

questions.q: A checkout adds a login step. What does this log?
questions.why: `toSpliced` is the non-mutating twin of `splice` (ES2023): it returns a new array with the change and leaves the original alone. Unlike `splice` it returns the new array, not the removed items.
questions.asked: It checks you know the ES2023 copy methods that make immutable updates readable.

questions.why: `reverse` reverses in place and returns the same array, so `newest` and `log` are one object and the push shows up in both. `toReversed()` returns a copy instead.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to test whether you know which array methods return the same reference.

questions.why: `for...in` iterates property keys, and array indexes are string keys, so the loop concatenates `'0'` and `'1'` onto the number 0, producing the string `001`. Use `for...of` for values.
questions.asked: It checks you know `for...in` is for object keys and why it should not be used on arrays.

questions.why: `entries()` yields `[index, value]` pairs, which destructure neatly in `for...of`. It is the loop equivalent of `forEach((name, i) => ...)`, but you can still `break` out of it.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions `entries()` when asked how to get the index in a `for...of` loop.

questions.q: A job queue gains items while it is being processed. What does this log?
questions.why: `forEach` fixes the number of iterations from the length when it starts, so items pushed during the loop are not visited. Mutating an array while iterating it is still best avoided, because removals do shift what is visited.
questions.asked: It checks you can reason about mutation during iteration instead of guessing.

questions.why: `some` stops at the first callback that returns truthy and returns a boolean, so the third item is never checked. `every` short-circuits the same way on the first falsy result.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because `some`/`every` are the idiomatic early-exit alternatives to `forEach`.

questions.why: The right-hand array is built first from the current values, then destructured into `a` and `b`, which swaps them without a temporary variable.
questions.asked: A quick check of array destructuring into existing variables.

questions.q: An API returned `{ data: null }`. What does this log?
questions.code:
const res = { data: null };
try { const { data: { user } } = res; } catch (e) { console.log(e.name); }
questions.why: Nested destructuring reads `user` from `res.data`, and destructuring `null` or `undefined` throws a TypeError. A default only applies to `undefined`, so `{ data: { user } = {} }` would still throw for `null`.
questions.asked: A strong answer points out that defaults do not protect against `null`, which is what JSON APIs send.

questions.code:
function paginate({ page = 1, size = 20 } = {}) { return `${page}/${size}`; }
console.log(paginate(), paginate({ size: 50 }), paginate({ page: null }));
choices: It throws on the first call
questions.why: The `= {}` default lets the function be called with no argument at all; without it, destructuring `undefined` throws. Property defaults apply only when a value is `undefined`, so an explicit `null` page passes through.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you know both layers of defaults in an options-object signature.

questions.code:
const [first, , third = 'n/a', ...others] = ['a', 'b'];
console.log(first, third, others);
questions.why: The empty slot skips `b`, `third` has no value so its default is used, and a rest element always produces an array, empty when nothing is left.
questions.asked: It checks you can read compact destructuring that appears in parsers and hooks.

questions.code: console.log([...'hello'].length, new Set('hello').size);
questions.why: Strings are iterable, so spread and `new Set` both see the characters; the Set keeps one `l`. Passing a string to `new Set` is a common accident when someone meant `new Set([str])`.
questions.asked: A quick check of iterables, and of a bug where a Set of words becomes a Set of letters.

questions.why: `arguments` is an array-like object: it has indexes and `length` but no array methods. Convert with `Array.from(arguments)`, or better, use rest parameters.
questions.asked: It checks you know the difference between array-likes and real arrays, which also applies to DOM collections.

questions.code: console.log(Array.from({ length: 2, 0: 'a', 1: 'b' }), Array.from({ 0: 'a' }));
questions.why: `Array.from` accepts iterables or array-likes; for an array-like it reads indexes up to `length`. The second object has no `length`, which counts as 0, so the result is empty.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see whether you know what makes an object "array-like".

questions.code:
const selected = [{ id: 1 }];
console.log(selected.includes({ id: 1 }), selected.some((s) => s.id === 1));
questions.why: `includes` compares by identity (SameValueZero), and the literal creates a brand new object, so it is not found. To check by content, compare the relevant field with `some`.
questions.asked: It is the array form of the "objects compare by reference" question, which drives every selection-state bug.

questions.q: A "seen" lookup is keyed by user objects. What does this log?
questions.why: Plain-object keys are always strings (or symbols), so both objects are converted to `[object Object]` and the second write overwrites the first. Use a `Map` (or `WeakMap`) when the key is an object.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to lead into "when would you use a Map instead of an object?".

questions.code:
const stock = { 1: 'in', '2': 'out' };
console.log(stock['1'], stock[2], Object.keys(stock));
questions.why: Property keys are converted to strings, so `1` and `'1'` name the same property and number lookups work. `Object.keys` therefore always returns strings, which matters when you then compare with `===`.
questions.asked: It checks you know why ids read back from `Object.keys` need converting before comparing to numbers.

questions.why: Square brackets in an object literal make a computed key: the expression is evaluated and its string value used. This is the standard way to build form-error objects keyed by field name.
questions.asked: A quick check of syntax that appears in every form handler and reducer.

questions.q: Empty query parameters are stripped before building a URL. What does this log?
questions.why: `Object.entries` turns the object into `[key, value]` pairs, `filter` drops falsy values, and `Object.fromEntries` rebuilds an object. Be careful: a legitimate `0` or `false` would be dropped too.
questions.asked: Interviewers like the entries → transform → fromEntries round trip as the idiomatic object "map/filter".

questions.why: `Object.assign` copies by assignment, so it triggers setters on the target, which stores 500 in `_t`. Spread into a new literal would instead define plain properties and never call a setter. The accessor `total` is itself an own enumerable key.
questions.asked: A strong answer contrasts `Object.assign` (assigns) with spread (defines), which matters for class instances and models.

questions.why: Spread copies only own enumerable properties into a plain object; methods live on `Money.prototype`, so `format` is not copied and `copy` is no longer a Money. Use a method such as `withPence()` that constructs a new instance.
questions.asked: It catches the bug where spreading a class instance into state silently drops its behaviour.

questions.code:
const settings = { theme: undefined };
console.log('theme' in settings, settings.theme !== undefined, 'toString' in settings);
questions.why: `in` checks whether a property exists, own or inherited, regardless of its value, so `theme` exists even though it is `undefined`, and `toString` is found on `Object.prototype`. Use `Object.hasOwn` to exclude inherited keys.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you can tell "missing" from "present but undefined".

questions.why: `JSON.stringify` drops properties whose value is `undefined`, so both serialise to `{"name":"Ada"}`. In memory they still differ: `a` has a `phone` key, which matters for `in`, `Object.keys` and PATCH semantics.
questions.asked: A strong answer relates this to PATCH requests, where "absent" and "null" must mean different things.

questions.q: What does this log in Node 24?
questions.why: `Object.groupBy` returns a null-prototype object, so there are no inherited methods such as `hasOwnProperty`, and a group called `constructor` cannot collide with anything. Use `Object.hasOwn(g, key)` to test for a group.
questions.asked: It checks you know the result is deliberately prototype-free, and why that is safer for user-supplied keys.

questions.q: Tasks are grouped by their owner object. What does this log?
questions.why: `Map.groupBy` keeps keys as they are, so both tasks go under the same object key. `Object.groupBy` would have converted the owner to the string `[object Object]`.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear when to pick `Map.groupBy` over `Object.groupBy`.

questions.q: Which is a correct shallow equality check for two flat objects?
choices: Check that every key of `a` has the same value in `b`
Check equal key counts, then every key of `a` against `b` with `Object.is`
questions.why: You need both the key count (otherwise extra keys in `b` are missed) and a per-key comparison. JSON comparison depends on key order and drops `undefined`, and checking only the keys of `a` ignores keys that only `b` has.
questions.asked: This is how `React.memo` and many selectors decide whether props changed, so interviewers like candidates who can write it.

questions.q: In a CommonJS script without "use strict", what does this log?
questions.why: `Object.freeze` is shallow: `port` is read-only (the write silently fails in sloppy mode), but `db` is a separate object that is not frozen, so its `host` changes. Freeze nested objects recursively if you need deep immutability.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions a deep-freeze helper or TypeScript `readonly` types as compile-time alternatives.

questions.q: What does this log in Node 24?
choices: It throws on the circular reference
questions.why: `structuredClone` deep-copies Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays and circular references correctly, which the JSON round trip cannot. The cycle is preserved inside the copy, pointing at the copy rather than the original.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear `structuredClone` as the modern default for deep copies, with its limits.

questions.q: A form draft is copied two ways before editing. What does this log?
questions.why: Spread copies only the top level, so `shallow.tags` is the same array as `draft.tags` and sees the push. `structuredClone` copies nested arrays and objects too, so `deep` keeps its own one-item array.
questions.asked: It is the simplest way to show you know the difference between shallow and deep copies.

questions.why: `structuredClone` copies own data properties into a plain object; the prototype link to `Money` is not preserved, so methods and `instanceof` are lost. Classes need their own `clone()` method.
questions.asked: A strong answer names this as the main reason `structuredClone` is not a universal copy for domain objects.

questions.q: How do you make a nested configuration object fully read-only at runtime?
choices: Declare it with `const`, which freezes every nested level
Call `Object.seal` once, which protects nested objects
Recursively `Object.freeze` each nested object as well
Call `Object.freeze` once, which recurses into children
questions.why: `Object.freeze` only affects the object you pass it, so a deep freeze walks the tree and freezes every nested object. `const` only stops the variable being reassigned, and `seal` is shallow too.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to check you know freezing is shallow, and when compile-time `readonly` types are enough.

questions.q: Which returns a new state with `user.address.city` set to `'Leeds'`, without mutating `state` and without losing other fields?
questions.why: Every object on the path to the change must be copied, and each copy must spread its original to keep sibling fields. The first option drops everything else in `user`, the third adds a literal dotted key, and `Object.assign(state, ...)` mutates `state`.
questions.asked: This is the core of reducer code; a strong answer mentions Immer or flatter state shapes when the nesting gets deep.

questions.q: A todo is marked done. What does this log?
questions.why: `map` makes a new array; unchanged items are reused by reference and only the edited item is replaced with a copy, so the original todo stays `false`. That structural sharing lets memoised rows skip re-rendering.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you can update an item by id immutably, the bread-and-butter of CRUD UIs.

questions.q: Which removes the todo with id `id` from `todos` without mutating it?
questions.why: `filter` returns a new array without the matching item. `splice` mutates (and `indexOf(id)` searches for the number, not an object with that id), `delete` leaves a hole, and `pop` ignores its argument and removes the last item.
questions.asked: A basic check that you can write the "delete" half of a CRUD list update.

questions.q: A reducer does `state.items.push(item); return state;`. Why does the React component not re-render?
choices: React compares old and new state with `Object.is`, and it is the same object
`push` is asynchronous, so the new item arrives after rendering
React deep-freezes state, so `push` throws and is swallowed
Reducers must return an array, not an object containing one
questions.why: React bails out when the next state is the same reference as the previous one, so an in-place mutation looks like "no change". Return a new object with a new array: `{ ...state, items: [...state.items, item] }`.
questions.asked: It is the single most common React state bug, and interviewers want the reference-equality explanation.

questions.q: With Immer, `produce(state, (draft) => { draft.items.push(x); })` looks like mutation. What actually happens?
choices: `state` is mutated in place and then frozen for safety
Immer deep-clones the whole `state` before running the recipe
Changes are recorded on a proxy; a new object shares untouched branches
The recipe runs later on a worker thread and returns a promise
questions.why: Immer gives you a proxy draft, tracks what you change, and builds a new state that copies only the changed path while reusing unchanged subtrees. The original is never modified, and there is no full deep clone.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions structural sharing and why it keeps both performance and reference-equality checks working.

questions.why: The spread copies the top level, so `next.user` still points at the same user object, while `cart` is replaced with a new object. Components that depend only on `user` can therefore skip re-rendering.
questions.asked: It checks you understand which references change in an immutable update.

questions.why: Map keys use SameValueZero: `NaN` equals `NaN` (unlike `===`) and `-0` equals `0`. `set` returns the map, which is why the calls chain.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see whether you know the equality rule Maps, Sets and `includes` share.

questions.q: A Map cache is keyed by a filter object. What does this log?
questions.why: Object keys are matched by identity, and the second literal is a different object, so the lookup misses. Keep a reference to the key object, or key by a primitive such as the id.
questions.asked: It checks the basic rule behind every "why is my Map cache always missing?" bug.

questions.why: A Map keeps the key's type, so the number 1 and the string `'1'` are different keys. An object converts every key to a string, so both spellings hit the same property. Watch for this when keys come from URLs or `Object.keys`.
questions.asked: It shows whether you would catch the bug of storing numeric ids and looking them up with route-parameter strings.

questions.why: `new Map(Object.entries(obj))` copies the pairs into a new Map, so changing the Map does not touch the object; `Object.fromEntries` accepts any iterable of pairs, including a Map.
questions.asked: A quick check that you can convert between objects and Maps in both directions.

questions.why: Maps iterate in insertion order, and updating an existing key keeps its original position. Only deleting and re-adding a key moves it to the end.
questions.asked: It checks you know Maps have a reliable order, unlike the integer-key reordering of plain objects.

questions.why: Bracket assignment creates an ordinary property on the Map object, not an entry, so `get` and `size` do not see it. Always use `set`/`get` with Maps.
questions.asked: It catches a common slip when someone switches an object to a Map and forgets to update the writes.

questions.q: A permission check uses the ES2025 Set methods. What does this log in Node 24?
questions.why: `difference` returns a new Set with the elements of `required` that are not in `granted`, i.e. the missing permission. `required` is not a subset of `granted` because `write` is missing; `granted.isSubsetOf(required)` would be true.
questions.asked: Interviewers like candidates who know the new Set methods replace hand-written filter loops.

questions.q: Duplicate rows are removed by id, keeping the latest. What does this log?
questions.why: Building a Map from `[id, row]` pairs lets later rows overwrite earlier ones with the same id, but an updated key keeps its first position. So id 1 stays first holding row `c`, followed by `b`.
questions.asked: A strong answer can say which duplicate wins and where it ends up, not just that duplicates are removed.

questions.why: `push` mutates the array and returns the new length, not the array. Code such as `setItems(items.push(x))` therefore stores a number; use `[...items, x]` instead.
questions.asked: It catches the React bug where state becomes a number after a push.

questions.why: `map` builds and returns a new array from the callback results; `forEach` exists only for side effects and always returns `undefined`. Neither changes the original strings.
questions.asked: A basic check that you pick `map` when you need a result and `forEach` only for effects.

questions.code:
const roles = ['Admin', 'Editor'];
console.log(roles.includes('admin'), roles.indexOf('Editor'));
questions.why: `includes` and `indexOf` compare strings exactly, so case matters; normalise both sides (e.g. `toLowerCase()`) for case-insensitive checks. Indexes start at 0, so `Editor` is at 1.
questions.asked: It checks you would not assume a role check is case-insensitive.

questions.code: console.log(['a', 'b', 'c'].join(), String(['a', ['b', 'c']]));
questions.why: `join()` uses a comma by default, and converting an array to a string calls `join()` recursively on nested arrays, so the nesting disappears. Pass `''` or `' '` explicitly when you want another separator.
questions.asked: A quick check of defaults that often surface in CSV exports and log lines.

questions.why: Writing to index 4 sets `length` to 5 and leaves holes at 0–3, which read as `undefined`. Arrays are not fixed-size and never throw for out-of-range writes.
questions.asked: It checks you understand that `length` is one more than the highest index, not a count of values.

questions.code: console.log(Object.entries(['x', 'y']));
questions.why: Arrays are objects whose indexes are string keys, so `Object.entries` returns `['0', 'x']` pairs with string indexes. `array.entries()` instead yields numeric indexes.
questions.asked: It shows whether you know array indexes are really string property names.

questions.q: User preferences are merged with defaults. What does this log?
questions.why: Later spreads win, so the defaults overwrite the user's choice; the key order comes from where `lang` was first defined. Put `...defaults` first and `...user` last.
questions.asked: It catches the most common merge-order bug in settings and options code.

questions.q: Which reliably checks that a plain object `filters` has no own properties?
questions.why: `Object.keys` lists own enumerable keys, so an empty result means no filters are set. Comparing with `{}` compares references (always false), an empty object is truthy, and objects have no `length`.
questions.asked: A basic check that shows you know objects are truthy and compared by reference.

questions.q: A search endpoint returned an empty page. What does this log?
questions.code:
const res = { items: [] };
console.log(res.items[0]?.name, res.items?.length, res.tags?.[0]);
questions.why: `items[0]` is `undefined`, so `?.name` short-circuits; `items` exists, so its length is 0; `tags` is missing, so `?.[0]` short-circuits. Use `?.[index]` for optional arrays.
questions.asked: It checks you can use optional chaining with array indexes, not just dotted properties.

questions.code:
const { id: userId, role: userRole = 'viewer' } = { id: 7, role: null };
console.log(userId, userRole);
questions.why: `id: userId` renames the property into a new variable, and a default is used only for `undefined`, so the explicit `null` role is kept. Apply `?? 'viewer'` afterwards if `null` should also fall back.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because renaming plus defaults is common in props and API mapping code.

questions.q: A hand-written hook returns a value and a toggle. What does this log?
questions.why: Destructuring copies the primitive value into `on` at that moment; the closure updates its own `v`, which `on` is not linked to. That is why React re-runs the component to give you a fresh value.
questions.asked: It connects destructuring to the "stale value after setState" confusion that mid-level candidates should be able to explain.

questions.why: Object spread ignores `null` and `undefined`, but array spread needs an iterable and throws a TypeError for them. Guard array spreads with `...(extra ?? [])`.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows the two spreads use different protocols (own properties vs iteration).

questions.why: When `isAdmin` is false, the expression is `false`, and spreading a primitive boolean adds nothing (it has no own enumerable properties). This is the usual conditional-property idiom.
questions.asked: It checks you can read the conditional-spread idiom, which is everywhere in request builders.

questions.q: A blog feed must list the newest post first. What does this log?
questions.why: ISO dates compare correctly as strings, and swapping `b` and `a` in the comparator reverses the order. No Date parsing is needed for sorting.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because sorting API rows by date is a daily task and the string trick is a real shortcut.

questions.code: console.log([3, undefined, 1].sort(), ['b', undefined, 'a'].sort());
questions.why: `sort` always moves `undefined` values to the end without calling the comparator for them; everything else is compared (here as strings). That is why missing values collect at the bottom of a sorted table.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know how sorts treat missing values, a detail behind many table bugs.

questions.q: A basket total is computed in pence. What does this log?
questions.why: The reduction works in integer pence (398 + 150 = 548), which is exact, and converts to pounds only for display. That avoids float errors from adding decimal prices.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains why totals are computed in minor units before formatting.

questions.why: `Object.entries` gives `[key, value]` pairs; the comparator destructures the values to sort descending, and array destructuring takes the first pair, not just its key.
questions.asked: It checks you can combine entries, sorting and destructuring, a typical "top N" dashboard task.

questions.q: Word counts are built from 100,000 log lines like this. What is the problem?
choices: It is quadratic: every step copies the whole accumulator
It gives wrong counts, because spread drops existing keys
It throws once the object passes 65,536 keys
It is fine; engines optimise spread inside `reduce`
questions.why: Spreading the accumulator allocates a new object and copies every key on each iteration, so the work grows with the square of the number of distinct words. Mutating the local accumulator (`acc[w] = ...; return acc;`) is safe here because nothing else holds it.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows that immutability matters for shared state, not for a private accumulator inside one function.

questions.q: A loop checks `allowedIds.includes(row.id)` for 50,000 rows against 10,000 allowed ids. What is the usual fix?
choices: Sort `allowedIds` first so `includes` can stop early
Use `some` instead, which short-circuits on a match
Build `new Set(allowedIds)` once and call `has` per row
questions.why: `includes`, `indexOf` and `some` all scan the array, so the loop does up to 500 million comparisons. A Set lookup is effectively constant time, turning it into about 60,000 operations. Sorting does not help a linear scan.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see if you notice accidental O(n × m) work in ordinary CRUD code.

questions.why: A Set keeps the first occurrence of each value in insertion order and ignores duplicates, including the later `add(1)`. It does not sort.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know Sets preserve insertion order and are not sorted.

questions.q: Ids come from a URL as strings. What does this log?
questions.code:
const ids = new Set([1, 2]);
console.log(ids.has('1'), ids.has(Number('1')));
questions.why: Set membership uses SameValueZero, so the string `'1'` is not the number 1. Convert route or query parameters before looking them up.
questions.asked: It catches the type-mismatch bug that makes "is this selected?" checks always fail.

questions.q: A team roster changed. What does this log in Node 24?
questions.why: `symmetricDifference` returns values in exactly one of the two sets (who left and who joined). `isDisjointFrom` is true only when the sets share nothing, and both contain `grace`.
questions.asked: A strong answer maps these methods to real features such as "show who was added or removed".

questions.q: A Map is saved to storage and read back. What does this log?
questions.why: Spreading a Map gives an array of `[key, value]` pairs, which JSON can represent; `new Map()` accepts that array to rebuild it. Stringifying the Map directly would produce `{}`.
questions.asked: It checks you know how to persist a Map, since `JSON.stringify` silently loses its contents.

questions.q: Request timing data is stored per request object. What does this log?
questions.why: A WeakMap supports `get`, `set`, `has` and `delete` only: it has no `size` and cannot be iterated, because entries can disappear whenever their key is garbage-collected.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear why a WeakMap cannot be enumerated, not just that it cannot.

questions.code:
const wm = new WeakMap();
try { wm.set('user:1', 'Ada'); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name); }
questions.why: WeakMap keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols), because only they can be garbage-collected. A string key throws a TypeError: "Invalid value used as weak map key".
questions.asked: It checks you know what a WeakMap can be keyed by.

questions.q: When is `WeakRef` an appropriate tool in application code?
choices: To implement a session store that must survive restarts
To keep a React component mounted while it is off-screen
To guarantee an object is freed as soon as the last user is gone
For a cache of large, re-creatable objects where losing an entry is fine
questions.why: A WeakRef lets the engine collect its target whenever it likes, so it only suits optional caches where a miss simply recomputes. Garbage-collection timing is unpredictable, so correctness must never depend on it.
questions.asked: A strong answer warns that WeakRef is rarely needed and that behaviour can differ between engines and runs.

questions.q: Which is a good reason to keep a plain object rather than switching to a Map?
choices: It needs to be sent as JSON or read as a fixed-shape record
Its keys are user-supplied strings that may be `__proto__`
Entries are added and removed thousands of times a second
You need the number of entries without counting them
questions.why: Objects serialise to JSON directly and suit records with known fields. Maps are better for arbitrary user-supplied keys (no prototype collisions), frequent additions and removals, and a built-in `size`.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask "Map or object?" constantly; a strong answer gives criteria in both directions.

questions.code:
const m = new Map([['a', 1]]);
console.log(Object.keys(m), [...m.keys()]);
questions.why: Map entries are internal data, not properties, so `Object.keys`, `Object.entries` and `for...in` see nothing. Use the Map's own `keys()`, `values()` and `entries()` iterators.
questions.asked: It checks you would not reach for object helpers when a value is actually a Map.

questions.why: `Object.entries` gives iterable `[key, value]` pairs, which destructure in `for...of`. Only `ink` has a falsy quantity. Iterating the object directly with `for...of` would throw, because plain objects are not iterable.
questions.asked: A basic check of the idiomatic way to loop over an object's keys and values.

questions.why: `Object.assign` copies into its first argument and returns it, so the shared defaults object is mutated and every later caller sees `page: 2`. Pass an empty target: `Object.assign({}, defaults, overrides)` or use spread.
questions.asked: It catches a classic bug where module-level defaults get polluted by one request.

questions.why: `find` returns the element itself, not a copy, so changing `u` changes the object inside the array. Copy first (`{ ...u, name: 'Grace' }`) when the array is state.
questions.asked: It checks you know search methods hand back references, the root of many "state changed by itself" bugs.

questions.code: console.log(Array(3).length, Array.of(3).length, [3].length);
questions.why: `Array(n)` with a single number creates an empty array of that length, while `Array.of(3)` and the literal `[3]` create a one-element array containing 3. `Array.of` exists precisely to avoid that special case.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to test whether you know the `Array` constructor's one-number trap.

questions.why: Setting `length = 0` empties the array in place, and `view` refers to the same array, so it is empty too. Reassigning (`selected = []` with `let`) would create a new array and leave `view` untouched.
questions.asked: A strong answer contrasts clearing in place with reassigning, and says when each is what you want.

questions.q: A list of roles is frozen. What does this log?
questions.why: Array methods such as `push` throw a TypeError on a frozen array even in sloppy mode, because they are specified to throw when a write fails. A plain `roles[1] = 'admin'` in sloppy code would fail silently instead.
questions.asked: It checks you know frozen arrays fail loudly through methods, which makes accidental mutation easy to find.

questions.why: `with(index, value)` returns a copy with one element replaced and accepts negative indexes. Unlike bracket assignment, it cannot grow the array: an out-of-range index throws a RangeError.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows the ES2023 copy methods well enough to predict their edge cases.

questions.q: Which replaces the element at index `i` of `list` with `item`, without mutating `list`?
questions.why: `with(i, item)` returns a copy with exactly one element replaced. `toSpliced(i, 0, item)` inserts instead of replacing, `splice` mutates, and the last option assigns into a temporary copy and evaluates to `item`, not an array.
questions.asked: It checks you can pick the right ES2023 copy method for editing a row in a table.

questions.q: A drag-and-drop list moves an item. What does this log?
questions.why: The item is removed first, which shifts later items left, then inserted at index 2 of the shorter array. Mutating the local copy is fine; the caller's array is untouched.
questions.asked: Reordering is a common take-home task; interviewers check you can reason about indexes shifting after removal.

questions.q: A React component keeps selected ids in a `Set` in state. Which updater toggles `id` correctly?
choices: Return `prev.add(id)`, since `add` returns the Set itself
Copy with `new Set(prev)`, add or delete on the copy, return the copy
questions.why: React needs a new reference to see a change, so copy the Set, change the copy and return it. Returning the mutated `prev` (or what `add` returns, which is the same Set) is invisible to React, and adding before copying has already mutated the old state.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because Sets and Maps in state trip up people who only know object spread.

questions.why: Page 3 starts at index 20 and `slice` stops at the end of the array without padding, so the last page simply has three rows. The same offset formula is what `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` pagination uses.
questions.asked: It checks the pagination arithmetic that every list screen and API needs.

questions.q: Records are sent to an API in batches. What does this log?
questions.why: `Math.ceil` makes room for a final partial chunk, and `slice` never pads past the end, so the last chunk holds just `e`. This helper is handy for batching API calls or database inserts.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions a real use, such as sending records in batches of 100.

questions.q: Rows are de-duplicated by email. What does this log?
questions.why: `seen.add` returns the Set, which is truthy, so the filter keeps the first row for each email and records it. The comparison is case-sensitive, so `A@x.io` counts as different; normalise with `toLowerCase()` for emails.
questions.asked: It checks you can read the compact filter-with-Set idiom and spot the case-sensitivity bug.

questions.why: `util.isDeepStrictEqual` compares structure and values recursively with strict equality, so the matching nested arrays are equal but `1` and `'1'` are not. It is the same check `assert.deepStrictEqual` uses.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that Node ships a deep-equality helper, so you do not reach for `JSON.stringify`.

questions.why: With `==`, an array compared to a string is converted to a string with `join(',')`, so the first and last are true. `===` between two array literals compares two different references, so it is false.
questions.asked: It checks you know why arrays must be compared element by element, not with `==` or `===`.

questions.q: Ids arrive as strings. What does this log?
questions.code:
const ids = ['10', '9', '100'];
console.log(ids.toSorted(), ids.toSorted((a, b) => a - b));
questions.why: The default sort compares strings character by character, so `'100'` comes before `'9'`. The subtraction comparator coerces both strings to numbers, giving numeric order.
questions.asked: A basic check that you never trust the default sort for numeric values, even when they are strings.

questions.why: Object spread copies own enumerable symbol-keyed properties as well as string keys, so `b[ID]` is 7. `JSON.stringify` ignores symbol keys, so they never appear in the JSON.
questions.asked: It separates people who know exactly what spread copies from those who assume "string keys only".

questions.code:
const users = [{ name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }, { name: 'Bo' }];
for (const { name, role = 'user' } of users) console.log(`${name}:${role}`);
questions.why: Destructuring works in the `for...of` binding, and the default applies to the missing `role`. It is a tidy way to normalise optional fields while looping.
questions.asked: A quick check of destructuring outside function parameters.

questions.code:
const a = ['x', , 'z'];
console.log([...a.keys()], Object.keys(a));
questions.why: The `keys()` iterator walks every index up to `length`, holes included, and yields numbers. `Object.keys` lists only properties that exist, as strings, so the hole at index 1 is missing.
questions.asked: It checks you understand that holes are missing properties rather than `undefined` values.

questions.q: A tic-tac-toe `board` is an array of row arrays. Which copy lets you set `next[0][0]` without changing `board`?
questions.why: The row arrays are nested references, so the copy must copy each row too. Spread, `slice` and `Object.assign` all copy one level, leaving `next[0]` pointing at the same row as `board[0]`.
questions.asked: Interviewers like the 2D grid version because it makes the shallow-copy trap concrete.

questions.why: Spreading reads the frozen object's values into a brand new object, which is not frozen, and the later `qty` overrides the copied one. Freezing only stops changes to that specific object.
questions.asked: It checks you know immutable updates are about making new objects, which works fine with frozen sources.

questions.q: A React component holds a `Map` in state. Which update is correct?
questions.why: Copy the Map and set on the copy; `set` returns the Map, so the new reference is what gets stored. The mutating versions pass the same reference, so React skips the render, and spreading a Map produces an empty plain object.
questions.asked: It checks you can apply immutable updates to collection types, not just to objects and arrays.

questions.q: What does this log in Node 24?
questions.why: `Object.groupBy` builds arrays per priority; `entries`/`map`/`fromEntries` then replaces each array with its length. For counts alone a single `reduce` is also fine, but this reads clearly.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows when `groupBy` helps and when a counting `reduce` is simpler.

questions.q: What does this log in Node 24?
questions.code:
const g = Object.groupBy([{ s: 'open' }], (x) => x.s);
console.log(g.closed?.length ?? 0, Object.keys(g));
questions.why: `groupBy` only creates keys for groups that actually occur, so `closed` is missing and needs `?.`/`??` handling. Pre-fill expected groups yourself if the UI must show zero counts.
questions.asked: It checks you handle empty groups instead of assuming every status key exists.

questions.q: Coordinate pairs are de-duplicated. What does this log?
questions.why: Arrays are compared by reference, so a Set of arrays would keep all three. Turning each pair into a string key gives the Set primitives to compare, and `1:2` and `2:1` are different strings.
questions.asked: It checks you know how to deduplicate compound values with a string key.

questions.code:
const o = { b: 1, '10': 1, '01': 1, 2: 1, '-1': 1 };
console.log(Object.keys(o).join(' '));
questions.why: Only canonical array-index keys (non-negative integers without leading zeros) are listed first, in numeric order; `'01'` and `'-1'` are ordinary string keys and keep insertion order after `b`.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know the exact ordering rule, which matters when object keys are ids or codes.

questions.why: Two Date objects are different references, so `includes` never finds a new one. Compare their timestamps instead, or store dates as ISO strings or numbers when you need `includes`/`Set` lookups.
questions.asked: It catches the "is this day a holiday?" bug that shows up in booking forms.

questions.why: The function receives a reference to the caller's object and mutates it, then returns that same object. Return `{ ...order, total }` if the caller's data must stay untouched.
questions.asked: It checks you would spot a helper with a hidden side effect on its argument.

questions.why: `toSorted` builds a new array, so it works on a frozen source. `sort` writes back into the array, and the frozen array makes that write throw a TypeError.
questions.asked: A strong answer uses this to argue for the ES2023 copy methods on shared or frozen data.

questions.code:
const prices = new Map([['tea', 250], ['cake', 300]]);
for (const [item, pence] of prices) console.log(item, pence / 100);
choices: It throws: a Map is not iterable
questions.why: Iterating a Map yields `[key, value]` entries in insertion order, which destructure directly in the loop. Maps are iterable, unlike plain objects.
questions.asked: A quick check that you can loop over a Map idiomatically.

questions.code: console.log(Object.fromEntries([['a', 1], ['b', 2], ['a', 3]]));
choices: It throws on the duplicate key
questions.why: Each pair is assigned in order, so a later duplicate overwrites the value but the key keeps its original position. Watch for this when turning query strings with repeated keys into objects.
questions.asked: It connects to `URLSearchParams`, where repeated keys silently collapse when converted to an object.

questions.code:
const m = new Map([['tea', 250]]);
m.forEach((a, b) => console.log(a, b));
questions.why: `Map.prototype.forEach` calls back with `(value, key, map)`, mirroring arrays' `(element, index, array)`, so the first parameter is the value. `for (const [key, value] of m)` gives the opposite order, which is why mixing the two causes swapped-argument bugs.
questions.asked: It catches a subtle bug when code switches between `forEach` and `for...of` over a Map.

questions.code:
const a = [1, , 3];
console.log([...a], a.slice());
questions.why: Spread uses the iterator, which reads holes as `undefined` and produces a dense array. `slice` copies properties by index and preserves the hole.
questions.asked: It separates people who know that "copy an array" has subtly different implementations.

questions.code: console.log(Object.assign({}, null, { a: 1 }, undefined, { a: 2, b: 3 }));
questions.why: `Object.assign` skips `null` and `undefined` sources and applies the rest left to right, so the later `a: 2` wins. Only a `null`/`undefined` target throws.
questions.asked: It checks you can safely merge optional option objects without guards.

questions.code:
const steps = ['Cart', 'Pay'];
console.log(steps.map((s, i) => `${i + 1}. ${s}`));
questions.why: `map` passes the index as the second argument, which is zero-based, so adding 1 gives human numbering.
questions.asked: A basic check that you know the callback signature of array methods.

questions.q: A card is added to a Kanban list immutably. What does this log?
questions.why: Each level on the path to the change is copied: the state, the lists array, the matching list and its cards array. The original cards array is untouched, so `state` still has one card.
questions.asked: It is the shape of every reducer in a board or cart app, so interviewers want you to write it fluently.

questions.code: console.log([[1], [2]].flatMap((x) => [x]));
questions.why: `flatMap` flattens exactly one level of what the callback returns. Each callback returns `[[1]]`-style arrays, so one level is removed and the inner arrays remain. Use `.flat(depth)` if you need more.
questions.asked: It checks you know `flatMap` is a map followed by `flat(1)`, not a full flatten.

questions.why: The parameter is a local variable holding a copy of the reference; reassigning it points the local at a new object and never touches the caller's `cart`. Mutating `cart.items` inside the function would have been visible.
questions.asked: It is the practical form of "is JavaScript pass-by-reference?".

choices: Yes: objects and arrays are passed by reference, primitives by value
No: everything is deep-copied, so functions never affect callers
No: it passes values, and for objects the value is a reference
Yes, but only for arrays; objects are copied one level deep
questions.why: JavaScript always passes by value, but the value of an object variable is a reference (often called call-by-sharing). So a function can mutate the caller's object, but reassigning the parameter never changes the caller's variable.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see if you can explain precisely why reassignment and mutation behave differently.

questions.why: `encodeURIComponent` encodes a space as `%20`, while `URLSearchParams` uses the form encoding, `+`. Servers decode both, and `URLSearchParams` also handles escaping for you.
questions.asked: A strong answer prefers `URLSearchParams` over hand-built query strings.
